lessons.title: Start Word and look around
lessons.html:
Microsoft Word is a program for writing documents: letters, lists, resumes, notes, and workplace forms. Microsoft’s guide for new users walks through how to start the program, find the main parts of the window, save your work, and format text.

To start Word on a Windows computer (Microsoft’s steps):

  1. Click the Start button, or press the Windows key, to open the Start menu.
  2. Find Word in the list of applications and click it.

The first time you start Word, a licence agreement might appear. Follow the on-screen choices with help from a tutor if you need it.

Useful parts of the window (from Microsoft’s tour):

  • The title bar shows the file name and the Word name, plus minimize, restore, and close.
  • The Quick Access Toolbar holds frequent commands such as Save, Undo, and Redo.
  • The File tab has commands that act on the whole document: New, Open, Save As, Print, and Close.
  • The ribbon holds the tools you use while writing. The Home tab is where you will find most text formatting.
  • The large white area is the edit window, where you type.
  • A scroll bar moves the page, and a zoom control changes how large the page looks.

To quit Word, click the X in the upper-right corner. If you changed the document since the last save, Word asks if you want to save. Click Yes to save, No to quit without saving, or Cancel if you clicked X by mistake.

This course is not MOS training and not a promise of a job.

lessons.title: Type and select text
lessons.html:
Click in the white page and start typing. Word wraps the text to the next line when you reach the end of a line, so you do not need to press Enter at the end of every line. Press Enter when you want a new paragraph.

Undo lives on the Quick Access Toolbar (Microsoft lists Undo and Redo there). If you delete something by mistake, try Undo right away.

To change text, select it first. Microsoft’s steps:

  1. Place the cursor at the beginning of the text you want to change.
  2. Press and hold the left mouse button.
  3. Drag to the right across the words. The selected text gets a coloured background.

Then you can delete the selection, type replacement words, or apply formatting (Lesson 3). To remove the selection, click once somewhere else on the page.

Practice ideas (your own words):

  • Write three short sentences about your week.
  • Write a two-line greeting, such as “Hello,” and your name.
  • Press Enter to start a new paragraph and add one more sentence.

Use Canadian spelling as you practise: centre, colour, cheque, favour. You will learn how to ask Word to check spelling in Lesson 5.

Do not type passwords, SINs, or other private numbers into a practice file on a shared computer.

If the page looks too small or too large, Microsoft’s tour includes a zoom control to change the view without changing the printed size of the words.

lessons.title: Format text on the Home tab
lessons.html:
Formatting changes how text looks so a letter or notice is easier to read.

Microsoft says most text formatting tools are on the Home tab, in the Font group. First select the text, then click a button.

Useful Font-group tools Microsoft lists:

  • Font and Font Size change the typeface and size.
  • Bold makes text thicker.
  • Italic slants the text.
  • Underline draws a line under the text.
  • Font Color changes the text colour.
  • Text Highlight Color looks like a highlighter pen.
  • Clear All Formatting removes extra formatting and leaves plain text.

Use formatting for a reason. A heading might be larger and bold. Important dates can be bold. Long stretches of coloured or underlined text are harder to read.

Styles apply a ready-made look to titles and headings. Microsoft’s steps:

  1. Highlight the text.
  2. On the Home tab, in the Styles group, point at a style to preview it.
  3. Click the style you want. Use the More arrow if you need to see more styles.

You can also change the look of the whole document from the Design tab, in Document Formatting, by pointing at a style set and then clicking it.

For line and paragraph spacing, Microsoft says to open the Design tab and choose Paragraph Spacing, preview a choice, then click it.

Save after you format so you keep the look you chose.

lessons.title: Save, open, and print
lessons.html:
You must save a document if you want to close Word without losing your writing. Microsoft says that when you save, the document is stored as a file on your computer or on a network location. Later you can open it, change it, and print it.

To save (Microsoft):

  1. Click the Save button on the Quick Access Toolbar.
  2. If you have saved this file before, Word saves it with the same name and you are done.
  3. If this is the first save, a Save As or “Save this file” window appears. Choose a location, type a name in the File name box, and click Save.

Use a clear name, such as cover-letter-practice or thank-you-note. Many people save into Documents. Microsoft notes that files may also sit in OneDrive or another location, depending on the computer’s setup.

To open a document later:

  • Open File Explorer, go to Documents (or the folder you used), and double-click the file, or
  • In Word, click the File tab, then Open. Recently saved files may appear under Recent.

To preview and print (Microsoft):

  1. Click the File tab.
  2. Click Print to see a preview.
  3. Review the settings.
  4. When the preview looks right, click Print.

Preview first. Ask learning-centre staff which printer to use. Saving often is safer than hoping you will remember at the end of class.

lessons.title: Check spelling the Canadian way
lessons.html:
This course uses Canadian spelling, such as centre, colour, cheque, and favour. Word can check spelling, but only in the language it is set to use.

Microsoft says you can manage the languages that check spelling and grammar.

For selected text:

  1. Select the words (or click in the paragraph).
  2. Go to the Review tab.
  3. Choose Language, then Set Proofing Language.
  4. Choose the language you want Word to use for that text.

Microsoft notes that languages already in use appear at the top of the list, and languages with downloaded proofing tools show a check mark. If you do not want Word to mark errors in selected text, you can choose not to check spelling or grammar for that selection.

To add a language or change the default:

  1. Go to Review > Language > Language preferences, or open File > Options > Language.
  2. Under authoring and proofing languages, you can add a language. If proofing tools are available, Microsoft shows a note such as Proofing available or Proofing installed.
  3. Follow the prompts to add the language and, if needed, get proofing tools.
  4. You can set a preferred authoring language.

Look for a Canadian English option if it appears on your computer. If you do not see it, ask a tutor — extra language or proofing tools may need to be installed.

If you write in more than one language, Microsoft describes a Detect language automatically check box under Review > Language > Set Proofing Language.

A spelling checker is a helper, not a judge. Read the suggestions before you accept them. This course is not an English-test credential.
